name: Thyrotoxicosis (uncomplicated)

matching.reasoningTemplate: Palpitations, weight loss and tachycardia with appetite preserved suggest thyrotoxicosis.

redFlags: Escalation to thyroid storm if fever/altered sensorium

clinicalPearls: Thyrotoxicosis (state of thyroid hormone excess) is NOT synonymous with hyperthyroidism (excessive thyroid gland function); destructive thyroiditis and ingestion of exogenous hormone cause thyrotoxicosis without true hyperthyroidism (p.3032).
Graves' disease accounts for 60-80% of thyrotoxicosis; affects up to 2% of women, ~10x less common in men, typically ages 20-50 (p.3032).
In the elderly, features may be subtle or masked, presenting mainly with fatigue and weight loss ('apathetic thyrotoxicosis'), and may be mistaken for depression (p.3033).
Weight loss occurs despite increased appetite due to raised metabolic rate, but ~5% of patients GAIN weight due to increased food intake (p.3033).
Atrial fibrillation is more common in patients >50 years; treating the thyrotoxic state alone reverts AF to sinus rhythm in up to 75% of those without underlying cardiac disease (p.3033).

Symptoms in descending frequency: hyperactivity/irritability, heat intolerance/sweating, palpitations, fatigue/weakness, weight loss with increased appetite, diarrhoea, polyuria, oligomenorrhoea/loss of libido (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Signs: tachycardia (AF in elderly), fine tremor, goitre, warm moist skin, proximal myopathy, lid retraction/lag (p.3033 Table 396-2).
Fine tremor is best elicited by having the patient stretch out the fingers while feeling the fingertips with the palm (p.3033).
Lid retraction (staring appearance) results from sympathetic overactivity and occurs in ANY form of thyrotoxicosis; it is distinct from the specific eye signs of Graves' ophthalmopathy (p.3033).

Graves' ophthalmopathy specific signs (proptosis, periorbital oedema, conjunctival injection, diplopia) occur in ~one-third of Graves' patients clinically; ~10% of ophthalmopathy is unilateral (p.3033-3034).
Graves' ophthalmopathy can occur in the absence of hyperthyroidism in ~10% (euthyroid ophthalmopathy); onset is within a year before/after thyrotoxicosis diagnosis in 75% (p.3034).
A diffuse, firm (non-nodular) goitre with a thrill or bruit at the inferolateral margins points to Graves' disease (p.3033).
Thyrotoxic hypokalaemic periodic paralysis is a recognised association, particularly common in Asian males (p.3033).

Mild hypercalcaemia occurs in up to 20% of patients (hypercalciuria more common) from thyroid-hormone-driven bone resorption; long-standing disease causes osteopenia and a small increased fracture rate (p.3033).
harrison.pathophysiology: Graves' hyperthyroidism is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSIs, detected as TSH-receptor antibodies/TRAb) that activate the TSH receptor. Susceptibility involves genetic (HLA-DR, CTLA-4, CD25, CD40, PTPN22, TSH-R gene) and environmental factors; concordance is 20-30% in monozygotic vs <5% in dizygotic twins. Triggers/risk factors include stress, smoking (moderate for Graves', major for ophthalmopathy), sudden iodine intake increases, the postpartum period (threefold rise), and immune reconstitution after HAART, alemtuzumab, or immune checkpoint inhibitors. Coexisting lymphocytic thyroiditis and TPO/Tg antibodies (up to 80%) mean there is no direct correlation between TSI level and hormone levels. Ophthalmopathy is driven by cytokine-mediated (IFN-gamma, TNF, IL-1) infiltration of extraocular muscles by activated T cells, fibroblast activation, glycosaminoglycan deposition trapping water, and aberrant IGF-1R signalling; the TSH-R is expressed in orbital tissue (p.3032-3033).
additionalDifferentials: Destructive thyroiditis: subacute (de Quervain) or silent/postpartum thyroiditis - transient thyrotoxic phase from preformed hormone release (p.3037)
Iodine excess (Jod-Basedow phenomenon); amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis in up to 10% (p.3032, 3034)
Struma ovarii and functional metastatic follicular carcinoma (ectopic thyroid tissue) (p.3032, 3037)
TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (secondary hyperthyroidism, inappropriately normal/high TSH) (p.3032, 3037)
Activating TSH-R mutation; activating GSalpha mutation (McCune-Albright) (p.3032)
Subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH, normal free T3/T4) (p.3034, 3041)
nonInfectiousMimics: Depression (especially apathetic thyrotoxicosis in the elderly) (p.3033)
additionalInvestigations: TRAb (TSH-receptor antibodies) - confirms Graves' when goitre/ophthalmopathy absent; useful for monitoring pregnant Graves' patients (high TSI crosses placenta -> neonatal thyrotoxicosis) (p.3033-3034)
Radionuclide (99mTc, 123I or 131I) scan and uptake - diffuse high uptake in Graves' vs LOW uptake in destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess, and factitious thyrotoxicosis (p.3034)
Color-flow Doppler ultrasonography - increased flow in hyperthyroidism vs destructive thyroiditis; avoids radioactivity (p.3034)
Unbound (free) T3 - to detect T3 toxicosis (2-5% of patients have only elevated T3) (p.3034)
TPO and thyroglobulin (Tg) antibodies; serum Tg increased in all thyrotoxicosis EXCEPT factitia (low in factitia, high in thyroiditis) (p.3033-3034, 3037)
Pituitary MRI/CT and alpha-subunit if TSH inappropriately non-suppressed (suspect TSH-secreting adenoma) (p.3034, 3037)
redFlags: Optic nerve compression at the orbital apex -> papilloedema, peripheral field defects and permanent vision loss; sight-threatening ophthalmopathy is an emergency (p.3034, 3036)
Corneal exposure/ulceration when lids fail to close during severe proptosis (p.3034)
Atrial fibrillation or worsening angina/heart failure, especially in elderly or pre-existing cardiac disease - high cardiac output can precipitate high-output failure (p.3033)
Features suggesting thyroid storm: fever, delirium, seizures, coma, vomiting, diarrhoea, jaundice (p.3036)
harrison.prognosis: Untreated, clinical features generally worsen; historical mortality was 10-30% before effective therapy. Mild Graves' may show spontaneous relapses and remissions, and rarely fluctuates between hypo- and hyperthyroidism with changing TRAb activity. About 15% of treated patients in remission develop hypothyroidism 10-15 years later from the destructive autoimmune process. Ophthalmopathy runs an independent course: typically worsens over 3-6 months, plateaus over 12-18 months, then partially improves (soft-tissue changes especially); fulminant in up to 5% requiring acute intervention. Thyrotoxic crisis carries 4-17% mortality even with treatment (p.3034-3036).
pitfalls: Do NOT assume thyrotoxicosis means hyperthyroidism - low radionuclide uptake indicates destructive thyroiditis, iodine excess or factitia rather than gland overactivity, which changes management (p.3032, 3037).

T3 toxicosis: 2-5% have suppressed TSH with elevated T3 but normal T4, so a normal T4 does not exclude thyrotoxicosis; conversely iodine-induced T4 toxicosis can show elevated T4 with normal T3 (p.3034).
Diagnostic confusion: thyrotoxicosis can elevate bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, and cause microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia (p.3034).

Antithyroid drug agranulocytosis (<1%) is idiosyncratic and abrupt - routine prospective blood-count monitoring is NOT useful; instead warn patients to stop the drug and obtain an urgent FBC for sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers (p.3036).

Suppressed TSH may persist for several months after starting antithyroid drugs, so TSH is not a reliable early index of response - titrate on unbound T4; euthyroidism is usually not reached until 6-8 weeks (p.3035).
Thyroid acropachy/clubbing without coincident dermopathy and ophthalmopathy in a Graves' patient should prompt a search for an alternative cause of clubbing (p.3034).
A normal TSH with normal unbound T4/T3 excludes thyrotoxicosis and excludes Graves' as the cause of a diffuse goitre (p.3034).
harrison.severityClassification: Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH with normal free T3 and free T4; treatment is increasingly recommended in the elderly to reduce atrial fibrillation and bone-loss risk (p.3034, 3041). Graves' ophthalmopathy severity is graded by the NO SPECS mnemonic (0 no signs/symptoms; 1 only signs e.g. lid retraction/lag; 2 soft tissue involvement; 3 proptosis >22 mm; 4 extraocular muscle involvement/diplopia; 5 corneal involvement; 6 sight loss), though activity-based systems such as EUGOGO are preferred for monitoring/treatment decisions (p.3034).
